title: Cell Division
notes:
Cell Cycle

Cell division is the process by which one cell divides to produce two or more daughter cells, passing on hereditary traits.

Basic characteristics of cells:

  • All cells arise from pre-existing cells.
  • Each cell has a definite life span.
  • Each cell's life span is called its cell cycle.
  • All cells are the same in genetic material but different in function.

Types of Cell Division

  • Amitosis: Direct cell division without chromosome formation.
  • Mitosis: Indirect or equational division.
  • Meiosis: Reductional division.

Interphase

Most metabolically active and longest phase of the cell cycle — the non-dividing stage.

Sub-phaseFull FormKey Events
G1Gap 1 / First Growth phaseCell growth; synthesis of RNA, proteins; cell becomes ready for DNA synthesis.
SSynthesis phaseDNA replication; each chromosome becomes two sister chromatids joined by a centromere; centrioles duplicate.
G2Gap 2 / Second Growth phaseSynthesis of proteins needed for cell division; preparation for M-phase.

Amitosis

Direct or simplest type of division observed in degenerated tissues, foetal membranes, certain yeast, protozoans, and cartilage cells.

Steps:

  • Nucleus elongates and constricts.
  • Nucleus divides into two parts without spindle formation.
  • Chromosomes are not formed.
  • Cytoplasm divides to produce two daughter cells.

Types:

  • Binary fission: Nucleus constricts into two parts and the organism divides into two (e.g., Amoeba).
  • Multiple fission: Nucleus divides repeatedly and many daughter cells form (e.g., Plasmodium).

Mitosis

Indirect division discovered by Walther Flemming (1882). Equal distribution of duplicated chromosomes — hence equational division.

Karyokinesis

Prophase

  • Chromosomes condense and appear as long, thin threads.
  • Centrioles move to opposite poles; spindle apparatus forms.
  • Nucleolus and nuclear membrane gradually disappear.

Metaphase

  • Chromosomes arrange on the equatorial plane (metaphase plate).
  • Each chromosome consists of two sister chromatids attached by a centromere.
  • Best stage to study chromosome morphology.

Anaphase

  • Centromeres divide; sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles.
  • Pulling and dragging movement of chromosomes.

Telophase

  • Chromosomes reach poles; nuclear membrane and nucleolus reappear.
  • Chromosomes uncoil back into chromatin fibers.

Cytokinesis

Division of cytoplasm after karyokinesis:

  • Cell plate method: Middle lamella forms from phragmoplast, dividing the cell — typical of plant cells.
  • Cleavage or furrowing method: Cytoplasm constricts from the periphery — typical of animal cells.

Significance of Mitosis

  • Growth of the organism from zygote to adult.
  • Repairs and replaces damaged and worn-out cells.
  • Helps in asexual reproduction.
  • Maintains genetic stability — each daughter cell gets an exact copy of chromosomes.

Meiosis

Reductional division occurring only in diploid reproductive cells (pollen mother cells, megaspore mother cells, spermatogonia, oogonia), producing haploid gametes.

Meiosis I (Reductional Division)

Prophase I (Longest)

Leptotene: Chromatin condenses into long, thin chromosomes.

Zygotene: Homologous chromosomes pair by synapsis, forming bivalents.

Pachytene: Bivalents shorten and thicken; crossing over (exchange of segments between non-sister chromatids) occurs.

Diplotene: Homologues begin to separate but remain joined at chiasmata.

Diakinesis: Terminalization of chiasmata; spindle formation; nuclear membrane and nucleolus disappear.

Metaphase I

Bivalents align on the equatorial plane; centromeres of each pair face opposite poles.

Anaphase I

Homologous chromosomes separate and move to opposite poles (centromeres do not divide).

Telophase I

Chromosomes reach poles; nucleolus and nuclear membrane reappear; followed by cytokinesis — two haploid cells form.

Meiosis II (Equational Division)

Similar to mitosis, but no DNA replication occurs before it:

  • Prophase II: Chromosomes condense.
  • Metaphase II: Chromosomes align on the equator.
  • Anaphase II: Sister chromatids separate.
  • Telophase II: Four haploid daughter cells form.

Significance of Meiosis

  • Reduces chromosome number to half, keeping it constant in the species.
  • Produces genetic variation through crossing over.
  • Plays a role in evolution.

examples:
**Q1: Interphase Events**

Which events occur in the G1, S, and G2 sub-phases of interphase?

**Solution:** G1 (first growth): synthesis of RNA and proteins, cell growth. S (synthesis): DNA replication — each chromosome becomes two sister chromatids joined by a centromere; centrioles duplicate. G2 (second growth): proteins needed for division are synthesized.

**Q2: Mitosis Stage Identification**

In which stage of mitosis do chromatids separate and move to opposite poles?

**Solution:** Anaphase. The centromeres divide, and sister chromatids are pulled to opposite poles.

**Q3: Cytokinesis Methods**

How does cytokinesis differ in plant and animal cells?

**Solution:** Plant cells divide by the cell plate method (middle lamella forms from the phragmoplast), while animal cells divide by cleavage or furrowing — the cytoplasm constricts from the periphery.

**Q4: Crossing Over**

During which substage of prophase I does crossing over occur, and what structure forms?

**Solution:** Pachytene. Exchange of segments between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes occurs; the exchange points are visible as chiasmata from diplotene.

**Q5: Chromosome Number**

A diploid cell with 2n = 20 undergoes meiosis. How many chromosomes are present in each daughter cell?

**Solution:** 10 chromosomes (n = 10). Meiosis is a reductional division; each of the four haploid gametes gets half the chromosome number.
keyPoints: Interphase = longest, most metabolically active phase: G1 (growth, RNA/protein synthesis), S (DNA replication, centriole duplication), G2 (division protein synthesis).
Mitosis (Walther Flemming 1882) = equational division; metaphase is the best stage to study chromosome morphology.
Cytokinesis: cell plate method in plant cells; cleavage/furrowing method in animal cells.
Meiosis = reductional division in diploid reproductive cells; produces 4 haploid gametes.
Prophase I (longest): Leptotene → Zygotene (synapsis, bivalents) → Pachytene (crossing over) → Diplotene (chiasmata) → Diakinesis (terminalization).
Anaphase I separates homologous chromosomes (centromeres do not divide); Anaphase II separates sister chromatids.
No DNA replication between Meiosis I and Meiosis II.
Meiosis maintains chromosome number across generations and creates genetic variation (crossing over).
summary: The cell cycle comprises interphase (G1, S, G2) and M-phase. Amitosis is direct division without chromosome formation. Mitosis (equational, Flemming 1882) — prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase plus cytokinesis (cell plate in plants, furrowing in animals) — gives identical daughter cells for growth, repair and asexual reproduction. Meiosis (reductional) occurs in diploid reproductive cells: Meiosis I halves chromosome number via synapsis (bivalents) and crossing over (chiasmata); Meiosis II is equational, producing 4 haploid gametes and genetic variation.
